transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Doc. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just feel like I’ve got this motor humming right under my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like, take our morning staff meetings at the building I clean. I’ve been doing maintenance there for a while now. It's a good gig, mostly, except for when the delivery guys leave the loading dock doors propped open and the stray cats get in. I spent half of Tuesday trying to coax this big orange tabby out from behind the main boiler. Kept trying to give it some tuna from my lunch, but it was just stubborn as all get-out. 

Anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the meetings. When I have to sit there, or like when I'm at the church event briefings on Sundays—which go on way too long because Pastor Dave loves the sound of his own voice—I just end up shifting in my chair the whole time. Eventually I just have to stand up in the back, or I'll find some excuse to go check the trash cans or move around. I just can't stay put.
Are you currently taking any medications, especially antipsychotics or anti-nausea drugs, and if so, did this restlessness start after beginning one of them?

No, I don't take anything like that. I mean, I take some ibuprofen sometimes for my knees, but that's about it. Being on my feet all day on those hard concrete floors down in the basement really does a number on your joints. Especially after I had to mop up the entire east wing last month when the pipes backed up. Man, what a mess that was. The plumber they called, this guy named Sal, he showed up two hours late and didn't even have the right size pipe wrench. I ended up having to let him borrow my own set from the maintenance closet. I've had that tool set since I finished my associate's degree, actually. My brother bought it for me as a graduation gift... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, pills. No, no antipsychotic things or nausea stuff. Just the ibuprofen.
Thinking back to when you were a kid in school, did you have similar trouble sitting still, staying focused, or following along with what was being said?

Yeah, actually... it's always been like this. I remember getting in trouble way back in grade school for popping out of my seat all the time. My mother used to say I acted like I was wound too tight, even as a little kid. I'd talk over the teacher, or I'd just rush ahead and start doing the assignment before they even finished giving the directions. 

I remember one time in fourth grade, Mrs. Gable's class. She was this older lady who always wore these bright floral dresses and had glasses on a chain around her neck. She had us doing this project where we had to build a diorama out of a shoebox. I brought in this really sturdy boots box that my dad's work boots came in. He worked at the auto plant over in the next town for thirty years. Anyway, I started gluing all these little plastic dinosaurs into the box before she even told us what the theme was supposed to be. Turns out it was supposed to be about the solar system. I had to paint over the dinosaurs to make them look like asteroids. Took me forever to get the paint out of my clothes, and my mom was so mad because she had just bought me those jeans for picture day... Wait, what was the question? Oh, yeah, school. Yeah, I had a lot of trouble sitting still and listening back then, too.

Aside from the restlessness, do you often find your mind wandering or losing track of what you're doing—like forgetting steps in a task or losing focus on conversations—even when nothing is distracting you?

No, not really. I mean, my mind doesn't just drift off into space or anything. If I'm doing something, I'm doing it. Like when I'm buffing the floors in the main lobby. You really have to pay attention to the buffer, you know? Those machines have a mind of their own if you don't hold them right. We got this new one last year, a real heavy-duty model, bright yellow. The old one was green and it had this squeak in the left wheel that drove me absolutely up the wall. I tried oiling it, taking the wheel off, everything. I even brought in some special grease my buddy Tom uses on his motorcycle. Tom's got this beautiful vintage Harley, spends every weekend polishing the chrome. We used to go riding up into the mountains back in our twenties, before he messed up his shoulder... but anyway, no, I don't really lose track of things. I just can't sit still while I'm doing them.
Do you often find yourself interrupting or talking over people, or blurting out answers or comments before someone finishes speaking, even when you don't mean to?

Yeah, I do that a lot, actually. It's like I just can't wait for them to get to the point. Like when my supervisor or one of the church staff starts giving me instructions for the week, I'll just jump right in with what I think they're going to say before they even finish their sentence. And sometimes I get it completely wrong, and they have to stop and correct me. It's kind of embarrassing, really. 

Like last Tuesday, Pastor Dave was trying to tell me about setting up the folding chairs for the choir practice. He started saying, "Make sure you put the chairs..." and I just blurted out, "In a circle in the fellowship hall, got it!" and turned around to walk away. But he actually wanted them in rows in the sanctuary because they were doing a special rehearsal with the organist. The organist, Mrs. Higgins, she's been playing there since I was a kid. She's got this little poodle that she brings to practice sometimes, sits right there in her purse on the bench. One time the dog got out and ran all over the altar, knocking over the communion cups... what a disaster. I had to steam clean the carpet in the front row. The steam cleaner we have at the church is this old clunky thing, not nearly as nice as the one I use at the office building. That one has a heated tank and everything... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, interrupting. Yeah, I do that a lot. I just get ahead of myself, I guess.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since grade school) pattern of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms: motor restlessness, inability to remain seated, blurting out answers/interrupting others, and acting before instructions are complete. These occur across multiple settings (work, church, historically school), causing functional/social friction (embarrassment, correction by supervisors/pastor). Inattentive symptoms (mind wandering, losing track of tasks, forgetting steps) are explicitly denied. No medication-induced akathisia or other substance-related cause identified. This pattern is consistent with ADHD, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Presentation (F90.1), rather than Combined (F90.2) or Predominantly Inattentive (F90.0) types.
